title: General Practical Physics I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 100L Practical Physics I curriculum: SI units and measurement, precision instruments (vernier caliper, micrometer screw gauge), error and uncertainty analysis, graph plotting technique, and standard first-year mechanics and heat experiments (simple pendulum, Hooke's law, density, specific heat capacity).

questions.question: The SI base unit of length is the:
options: Metre
Centimetre
Foot
Kilometre
questions.correct_answer: Metre
questions.explanation: The metre is the SI base unit of length; centimetres and kilometres are derived (non-base) multiples of it.

questions.question: Which of the following is a fundamental (base) SI quantity, as opposed to a derived quantity?
options: Mass
Velocity
Force
Density
questions.correct_answer: Mass
questions.explanation: Mass (measured in kilograms) is one of the seven SI base quantities; velocity, force, and density are all derived from combinations of base quantities.

questions.question: In an experiment, a student records a length as 12.30 cm rather than 12.3 cm. The extra trailing zero indicates that:
options: The measurement was made to a precision of 0.01 cm
The measurement is less precise than 12.3 cm
The zero is not a significant figure
An error was made in the measurement
questions.correct_answer: The measurement was made to a precision of 0.01 cm
questions.explanation: Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant figures; writing 12.30 cm instead of 12.3 cm communicates that the instrument could resolve to the hundredths place.

questions.question: A systematic error in an experiment is one that:
options: Consistently biases readings in the same direction and cannot be reduced by repeating the measurement
Varies randomly from one reading to the next
Can be eliminated by taking the average of many readings
Only occurs when the observer is careless
questions.correct_answer: Consistently biases readings in the same direction and cannot be reduced by repeating the measurement
questions.explanation: Systematic errors, such as a zero error on an instrument, consistently shift all readings in one direction; repeating the measurement does not remove them -- only correcting or recalibrating the instrument does.

questions.question: Random errors in a set of readings can generally be reduced by:
options: Taking several readings and calculating their average
Using a single reading and rounding it
Ignoring the smallest and largest readings only
Increasing the systematic error
questions.correct_answer: Taking several readings and calculating their average
questions.explanation: Random errors scatter unpredictably above and below the true value, so averaging multiple independent readings reduces their overall effect on the result.

questions.question: Which of these best describes the difference between accuracy and precision in measurement?
options: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is the closeness of repeated readings to each other
Accuracy and precision mean exactly the same thing
Precision is closeness to the true value; accuracy is the spread of repeated readings
Accuracy depends only on the number of decimal places recorded
questions.correct_answer: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is the closeness of repeated readings to each other
questions.explanation: A set of readings can be precise (tightly clustered) but inaccurate (offset from the true value due to systematic error), so the two concepts must be distinguished.

questions.question: The least count of a measuring instrument refers to:
options: The smallest measurement that can be accurately read from the instrument
The largest measurement the instrument can take
The average of all readings taken with the instrument
The zero error of the instrument
questions.correct_answer: The smallest measurement that can be accurately read from the instrument
questions.explanation: Least count is the smallest value an instrument can reliably resolve, e.g. 0.01 cm for a typical vernier caliper or 0.01 mm for a micrometer screw gauge.

questions.question: A vernier caliper with 10 divisions on its vernier scale matched against 9 divisions on the main scale (each 1 mm) has a least count of:
options: 0.1 mm
1 mm
10 mm
questions.correct_answer: 0.1 mm
questions.explanation: Least count = 1 main scale division / number of vernier divisions = 1 mm / 10 = 0.1 mm, the standard resolution of a common vernier caliper.

questions.question: The vernier caliper is most suitable for accurately measuring:
options: Internal and external diameters and depths of small objects
Very small thicknesses such as a sheet of paper
Large distances such as the length of a football field
Electrical resistance
questions.correct_answer: Internal and external diameters and depths of small objects
questions.explanation: A vernier caliper is designed with jaws and a depth probe to measure external dimensions, internal dimensions, and depths of small objects to a precision of about 0.01-0.1 mm.

questions.question: A micrometer screw gauge is typically used to measure:
options: Very small thicknesses or diameters, such as the diameter of a thin wire
The volume of a large container
The mass of an object
Long distances of several metres
questions.correct_answer: Very small thicknesses or diameters, such as the diameter of a thin wire
questions.explanation: The micrometer screw gauge has a finer least count than a vernier caliper (typically 0.01 mm), making it suitable for very small dimensions like wire diameter or sheet thickness.

questions.question: In a micrometer screw gauge, the pitch is the distance moved by the spindle per full rotation, and the least count is calculated as:
options: Pitch divided by the number of divisions on the circular (thimble) scale
Pitch multiplied by the number of divisions on the circular scale
Pitch divided by the main scale reading
The reciprocal of the pitch
questions.correct_answer: Pitch divided by the number of divisions on the circular (thimble) scale
questions.explanation: Least count of a micrometer screw gauge = pitch / number of divisions on the circular scale, giving the smallest measurable increment.

questions.question: Before taking readings with a vernier caliper or micrometer screw gauge, a student should first check for:
options: Zero error
The colour of the instrument
The brand of the instrument
The room temperature only
questions.correct_answer: Zero error
questions.explanation: Checking for zero error (the reading shown when the jaws/spindle are fully closed) is essential so it can be added to or subtracted from subsequent readings to correct for it.

questions.question: Parallax error in reading a scale, such as a metre rule, occurs when:
options: The observer's eye is not positioned perpendicular to the scale being read
The scale is not calibrated correctly
The object being measured moves during the reading
The reading is taken in poor lighting
questions.correct_answer: The observer's eye is not positioned perpendicular to the scale being read
questions.explanation: Parallax error arises from viewing a scale at an angle rather than directly perpendicular (at eye level with the pointer or meniscus), causing a misread value.

questions.question: When plotting a graph from experimental data, the independent variable (the one deliberately varied by the experimenter) is conventionally plotted on the:
options: Horizontal (x) axis
Vertical (y) axis
Either axis, it does not matter
Diagonal of the graph
questions.correct_answer: Horizontal (x) axis
questions.explanation: By convention, the independent variable that the experimenter controls is plotted on the x-axis, while the dependent variable being measured is plotted on the y-axis.

questions.question: When drawing a line of best fit through a scatter of experimental points, the line should:
options: Pass as close as possible to all the points, with roughly equal numbers of points above and below it
Always pass through every single data point exactly
Only connect the first and last data points
Always be forced through the origin regardless of the data
questions.correct_answer: Pass as close as possible to all the points, with roughly equal numbers of points above and below it
questions.explanation: A line of best fit is a smooth straight (or curved) line that best represents the overall trend of the data, minimising the scatter of points above and below it.

questions.question: On a straight-line graph of y against x, the gradient (slope) represents:
options: The rate of change of y with respect to x
The value of y when x is zero
The total area under the graph
The maximum value of x
questions.correct_answer: The rate of change of y with respect to x
questions.explanation: The gradient of a straight-line graph, calculated as (change in y)/(change in x), gives the rate at which y changes with x -- often representing a physical constant in an experiment.

questions.question: A student plots extension (y-axis) against load (x-axis) for a spring and obtains a straight line through the origin with gradient 0.02 m/N. What physical quantity does this gradient represent?
options: The reciprocal of the spring's force constant (1/k)
The spring's force constant k directly
The spring's natural length
The mass of the spring
questions.correct_answer: The reciprocal of the spring's force constant (1/k)
questions.explanation: Since extension e = F/k, plotting e against F gives a gradient of 1/k; the force constant k is therefore the reciprocal of the measured gradient.

questions.question: In a simple pendulum experiment to determine g, a graph of T^2 (y-axis) against length L (x-axis) is plotted. The gradient of this line equals:
options: 2*pi/g
g
questions.explanation: Since T^2 = (4*pi^2/g)L, plotting T^2 against L gives a straight line through the origin with gradient 4*pi^2/g, from which g can be calculated.

questions.question: In the simple pendulum experiment, why is the time for a large number of oscillations (e.g. 20) measured, rather than timing a single oscillation?
options: To reduce the percentage error caused by human reaction time in starting and stopping the stopwatch
Because a single oscillation cannot be timed at all
To increase the length of the pendulum
Because the pendulum only swings correctly after 20 oscillations
questions.correct_answer: To reduce the percentage error caused by human reaction time in starting and stopping the stopwatch
questions.explanation: Timing many oscillations and dividing by the number of oscillations spreads the fixed reaction-time error over a longer total time, reducing its percentage effect on the period measurement.

questions.question: In a simple pendulum experiment, which factor does NOT significantly affect the period of oscillation (for small angular displacements)?
options: The mass of the pendulum bob
The length of the pendulum
The acceleration due to gravity
None of the above -- all affect the period
questions.correct_answer: The mass of the pendulum bob
questions.explanation: For small-angle oscillations, the period T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) depends only on the pendulum's length and the local gravitational acceleration, not on the mass of the bob.

questions.question: In Hooke's law verification experiment, a spring is loaded with increasing masses and the extension recorded. The elastic limit is exceeded when:
options: The extension-load graph stops being a straight line and the spring no longer returns to its original length
The spring breaks immediately
The extension becomes exactly proportional to the load
The spring's colour changes
questions.correct_answer: The extension-load graph stops being a straight line and the spring no longer returns to its original length
questions.explanation: Beyond the elastic limit, the extension-load relationship deviates from Hooke's law linearity, and the spring undergoes permanent deformation, not returning to its original length when unloaded.

questions.question: To determine the density of an irregularly shaped solid that sinks in water, the volume is typically found by:
options: Measuring the volume of water it displaces when fully submerged
Using a metre rule to measure its length, width, and height
Weighing it in air only
Calculating it from its mass alone
questions.correct_answer: Measuring the volume of water it displaces when fully submerged
questions.explanation: For an irregular solid, volume is found using the displacement method (e.g. a eureka can or measuring cylinder), since its shape prevents direct geometric calculation.

questions.question: A solid has a mass of 45 g and displaces 15 cm^3 of water when fully submerged. What is its density?
options: 3 g/cm^3
questions.correct_answer: 3 g/cm^3
questions.explanation: Density = mass/volume = 45 g / 15 cm^3 = 3 g/cm^3.

questions.question: In an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block by the method of mixtures, the metal block is usually:
options: Heated to a known high temperature, then transferred quickly into cool water in a calorimeter
Left at room temperature throughout the experiment
Weighed after being placed in the water
Dissolved completely in the water
questions.correct_answer: Heated to a known high temperature, then transferred quickly into cool water in a calorimeter
questions.explanation: The metal block is heated to a measured temperature (often in boiling water), then quickly transferred into a calorimeter containing cooler water so the resulting temperature change can be used to calculate its specific heat capacity.

questions.question: In the method of mixtures experiment, why is the calorimeter usually made of a material like copper with a polished exterior?
options: Copper conducts heat well internally, while a polished exterior minimises heat loss by radiation
Copper is the cheapest available material
A polished surface increases heat loss to speed up the experiment
Copper is a good electrical insulator
questions.correct_answer: Copper conducts heat well internally, while a polished exterior minimises heat loss by radiation
questions.explanation: Copper has high thermal conductivity, allowing the calorimeter's contents to reach thermal equilibrium quickly, while a shiny outer surface reduces unwanted heat exchange with the surroundings by radiation.

questions.question: A student measures the length of a wire five times, obtaining 24.5, 24.6, 24.4, 24.6, and 24.5 cm. What is the mean value of these readings?
If the true value of a quantity is 10.0 cm and a measurement gives 9.8 cm, what is the percentage error in the measurement?
questions.explanation: Percentage error = |true value - measured value| / true value x 100% = 0.2/10.0 x 100% = 2%.

questions.question: In Boyle's law experiment using a J-tube apparatus, which two quantities are measured to verify the law?
options: The pressure of the trapped air column and its corresponding length (proportional to volume)
The temperature and mass of the trapped air
The colour and density of the trapped air
The weight of the mercury column only
questions.correct_answer: The pressure of the trapped air column and its corresponding length (proportional to volume)
questions.explanation: In the J-tube (or similar) Boyle's law apparatus, the length of the trapped air column (proportional to its volume, given constant cross-sectional area) is measured at different applied pressures, and a graph of P against 1/L verifies the inverse relationship.

questions.question: A graph of pressure P against 1/L (where L is the length of a trapped air column) for Boyle's law experiment should ideally produce:
options: A straight line through the origin
A curve that rises steeply then flattens
A horizontal straight line
A straight line that does not pass through the origin
questions.correct_answer: A straight line through the origin
questions.explanation: Since Boyle's law states P is proportional to 1/V (and L is proportional to V here), plotting P against 1/L should yield a straight line passing through the origin, confirming the inverse proportionality.

questions.question: When recording an experimental result, why should measured values always be reported with appropriate units?
options: Because a numerical value without units is physically meaningless
Units are optional and only added for decoration
Units only matter for electrical measurements
Units change the actual measured value
questions.correct_answer: Because a numerical value without units is physically meaningless
questions.explanation: A physical quantity is fully specified only by a number together with its unit; omitting units makes the measurement ambiguous and unusable for calculation or comparison.

questions.question: A stopwatch has a resolution of 0.01 s but the experimenter's reaction time introduces an uncertainty of about 0.2 s. The dominant source of uncertainty in timing a single short event here is:
options: Human reaction time, not the stopwatch's resolution
The stopwatch's resolution, not reaction time
Neither source contributes any uncertainty
The temperature of the room
questions.correct_answer: Human reaction time, not the stopwatch's resolution
questions.explanation: Since reaction time (about 0.2 s) is much larger than the stopwatch's resolution (0.01 s), it dominates the overall timing uncertainty for a single manually timed event.

questions.question: In a lab report, the purpose of recording a table of raw data before processing it is to:
options: Preserve the original measurements so calculations can be checked or redone if needed
Make the report longer
Replace the need for a graph
Avoid stating the aim of the experiment
questions.correct_answer: Preserve the original measurements so calculations can be checked or redone if needed
questions.explanation: Recording raw data in a clear table ensures transparency and allows calculations, graphs, and conclusions to be verified or recalculated if an error is suspected.

questions.question: Why should repeated readings be taken and averaged in most practical physics experiments?
options: To minimise the effect of random errors and obtain a more reliable value
To make the experiment take longer
Because a single reading is never physically possible
To eliminate all systematic errors automatically
questions.correct_answer: To minimise the effect of random errors and obtain a more reliable value
questions.explanation: Averaging several independent readings reduces the influence of random fluctuations, giving a value closer to the true one, although it does not remove systematic errors.

questions.question: A metre rule is used to measure the length of a wire, with its zero end aligned incorrectly 0.2 cm before the true zero mark. This introduces what type of error into every reading taken with it?
options: A systematic (zero) error
A random error
No error at all
An error only in the final reading
questions.correct_answer: A systematic (zero) error
questions.explanation: A misaligned zero mark causes every measurement taken with that rule to be offset by the same fixed amount in the same direction -- a classic systematic (zero) error.

questions.question: When reading the level of a liquid in a measuring cylinder, the reading should be taken at eye level from the:
options: Bottom of the meniscus (for most liquids like water)
Top of the meniscus always
Side of the cylinder, viewed from above
Widest point of the cylinder
questions.correct_answer: Bottom of the meniscus (for most liquids like water)
questions.explanation: For liquids such as water that wet glass and form a concave meniscus, the reading is conventionally taken at the bottom of the curve, viewed at eye level to avoid parallax error.

questions.question: In an experiment to determine acceleration due to gravity using a free-fall apparatus (e.g. ticker-tape timer or light gates), a graph of velocity against time is plotted. The gradient of this graph gives:
options: The acceleration due to gravity, g
The total distance fallen
The initial velocity
The mass of the falling object
questions.correct_answer: The acceleration due to gravity, g
questions.explanation: Since acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, the gradient of a velocity-time graph for a freely falling object gives the value of g.

questions.question: A ticker-tape timer commonly used in mechanics experiments in Nigerian university labs typically operates from the AC mains at a frequency of:
options: 50 Hz
1 Hz
500 Hz
5 Hz
questions.correct_answer: 50 Hz
questions.explanation: A ticker-tape timer makes dots on the tape at the frequency of the AC mains supply, which is 50 Hz in Nigeria, producing one dot every 1/50 = 0.02 s.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a control variable in a physics experiment, such as keeping the amplitude of a pendulum's swing small and constant?
options: To ensure that only the variable being investigated affects the results
To make the experiment take less time
To eliminate the need for repeated readings
To increase the systematic error deliberately
questions.correct_answer: To ensure that only the variable being investigated affects the results
questions.explanation: Controlling other variables (e.g. keeping the pendulum's swing angle small) isolates the effect of the variable being studied (e.g. length) on the outcome (period), ensuring a valid experiment.

questions.question: A student obtains inconsistent, widely scattered results for the period of a pendulum. This scatter is most likely due to:
options: Random errors, such as variation in reaction time when starting/stopping the stopwatch
A single large systematic error only
The pendulum having no mass
The pendulum string being too short to measure
questions.correct_answer: Random errors, such as variation in reaction time when starting/stopping the stopwatch
questions.explanation: Widely scattered (rather than consistently offset) results are typically caused by random errors, such as inconsistent reaction time, rather than a systematic bias.

questions.question: In a practical report, the 'precision' of a final calculated result should generally be expressed to:
options: The same number of significant figures as justified by the least precise measurement used in the calculation
As many decimal places as the calculator displays
Exactly two decimal places in all cases
Whole numbers only
questions.correct_answer: The same number of significant figures as justified by the least precise measurement used in the calculation
questions.explanation: A calculated result cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement that went into it, so the final answer's significant figures should reflect that limiting precision.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a zero error that must be subtracted from subsequent readings on a micrometer screw gauge?
options: The scale reads 0.02 mm when the jaws are fully closed with nothing between them
The scale reads exactly 0.00 mm when the jaws are fully closed
The object being measured has an irregular shape
The screw gauge is used to measure a rod instead of a wire
questions.correct_answer: The scale reads 0.02 mm when the jaws are fully closed with nothing between them
questions.explanation: If the instrument does not read exactly zero when fully closed, that offset (positive or negative) is the zero error, which must be corrected for in every subsequent reading.
